tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (Proc. ACM IMWUT 2(3), Article 93, 2018) compares Sprintz with SIMD-BP128, FastPFOR and Simple8b on ratio and decompression speed; the README names these baselines and links the harness (dblalock/lzbench fork, results/ directory), but no compiler flags or CPU model are stated on pages reachable here, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'state-of-the-art compression ratios, and can decompress at multiple GB/s in a single thread'; with 1KB and 10KB blocks 'Sprintz does even better relative to other methods'. Paper abstract (search snippet only; arXiv and ACM blocked): decompresses at up to 3GB/s in a single thread with under 1KB of memory. No per-codec numbers on the README page.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark harness and raw results live in the separate fork https://github.com/dblalock/lzbench (results/ucr, results/multicore, results/ndims_speed and others), not in the sprintz repo (sprintz/results returns 404); the numbers files were not opened, and the paper (arXiv, ACM) is blocked in this environment. FastPFor, SIMD-BP128 and Simple8b were run on 8/16-bit data zero-padded to 32 bits and their ratios divided by the padding factor (README says so), which favours the byte-aware Sprintz. README states the speed claim without CPU model or flags and says the code was only tested with Clang on OS X. Last commit 2021-01-10 (github.com commits page).

notes: Metadata matches: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file), 80 stars, 14 forks, not archived, last commit 2021-01-10, so abandoned is right. Paper venue is ACM IMWUT 2018 (DOI 10.1145/3264903, from search results). The benchmark harness is a fork of inikep/lzbench with 3 stars.

tier_reason: First-party README table from cargo bench on an Intel Core i5-8250U, one thread, comparing only its own scalar BitPacker1x layout with the SSE3 and AVX2 layouts; no compiler flags and no head-to-head with simdcomp, FastPFor or another external codec.

corrections.claimed_speedup: BitPacker1x: compress 1.4, compress_delta 1.0, decompress 1.8, decompress_delta 1.4 billion int/s. BitPacker4x (SSE3): compress 5.3, compress_delta 2.8, decompress 5.5, decompress_delta 5 billion int/s. BitPacker8x (AVX2): compress 7, compress_delta 0.6 (600 million), decompress 6.5, decompress_delta 5.6 billion int/s. README headline: 'Expect > 4 billions integers per seconds.' SSE3/AVX2 over BitPacker1x is about 3-5x for compress and decompress (derived from page data); BitPacker8x compress_delta is slower than scalar BitPacker1x (0.6 vs 1.0 billion int/s, derived from page data).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 341 stars, 37 forks; crates.io: 26.2 million downloads, 34 reverse dependencies including tantivy, tantivy-bitpacker, paradedb-tantivy, qdrant-edge, lance-bitpacking and chroma-types
corrections.caveats: No head-to-head against FastPFor, simdcomp, varint or Simple8b is shown; the only comparison is among its own three layouts (formats are mutually incompatible) and a remark that LZ4 is a poor fit. It is a Rust port of Lemire's simdcomp (README), which is already listed, so it adds Rust portability rather than a new algorithm. Compiler flags not given. The README's own table shows BitPacker8x compress_delta at 600 million int/s, below the scalar layout's 1.0 billion.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Tantivy usage confirmed via crates.io reverse dependencies. Port of the already-listed https://github.com/lemire/simdcomp: orchestrator may prefer decision duplicate per the ports rule.

tier_reason: First-party README numbers from its own bench_test.go, against the package's own scalar reference only; amd64 runs on unnamed CI runners and a QEMU VM, flags unstated, so C.

corrections.caveats: Baseline is the library's own scalar code, not simdcomp, FastPFor, varint or Simple8b; README says a head-to-head against ronanh/intcomp is only a follow-up. amd64 CI numbers come from shared ubuntu-latest runners with no CPU model, and the author's own QEMU re-bench gives lower ratios (17.8-24.0x). The scalar baseline (about 2.3 GB/s pack at 8 bits) is slow, which inflates the ratio. arm64 has no SIMD kernel (about 1.0x). Absolute GB/s figures are over the uint32 input stream. Output is byte-identical to simdcomp's SIMD_fastpackwithoutmask, so it is a Go reimplementation of the already-listed simdcomp format. Repository has 0 stars.

notes: All numbers match the README (amd64 CI table, QEMU re-bench, POWER9 7.0x/11.3x, z15 23x/34x). BSD-3-Clause confirmed from LICENSE; last commit 2026-09-08. Go reimplementation of the simdcomp layout; orchestrator may treat as a port.
